Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB427.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhulangsheng of Qingcheng. Zhulang Chesheng owns the retained deployment, having the whole world go into the retreat at once and come out with it, every dust and thing back in place.

Senses.Explanation: A fixed totality formula that sweeps the whole world, sky and ground, into one loaded stroke. Jieshi Zhipeng hangs the whole world on falling leaves that know autumn and riding the ox in search of the ox, Linye Tongqi gives the whole world to cold and then to heat and bars the seasons from the measureless one, Poshan Haiming at his old teacher's memorial serves heat that kills and cold that kills, and rules that so understood neither season nor birth and death can move one, Tianyin Yuanxiu fills it with light and fills it with dark, yet the light lights not itself nor the dark itself, and Mingjue Cong settles the patched monk's own native ground over the whole world, unmoved by season's shift and owing nothing to birth and death. Shanhui Huan lets the heat come with rhino-fan swatting gnats and pomegranate fire scorching the sky, and the cold with snow-pearls filling ditches and blue glass piling hills, Baiyu Jingsi reads the Samantabhadra range plugging ravines and brimming channels while the Shaolin true pulse rings the whole world, Baichi Xingyuan rolls back the thick clouds without a speck and the sun wheels up the jade tower while spring warmth fills the whole world and the black steer and dun colt grin, Faxi Yin opens the year with blessing clouds rising over the whole world at his wishing-the-sage hour, and Zhulang Chesheng has the whole world go into the retreat at once and come out with it, every dust and thing back in place.

Senses.Explanation: Communal tea as an announced occasion for the assembled community. The exact word usually belongs to a compiler or narrator’s occasion line—retreat tea, evening tea, or a tea-before-address heading—while the following speech belongs to the named master; one dialogue also names communal tea as a reason for sounding the drum.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a general address to the community
Senses.Explanation: A general address is a scheduled public address to the monastic community, announced and staged as its own recorded-sayings event. Chan records give it a placard, venue, occasion, audience, and sometimes questions, making ordinary broad speaking an institution. The Classified Essentials of the Patriarchs lists “ascending the hall, small gathering, address to the assembly, and general address” (上堂、小參、示眾、普說) as separate headings. The monastic code makes its organization explicit: a general-address placard is hung before the monks' hall and common quarters, a venue is prepared, and the drum is sounded after gruel. Records qualify an address by occasion, as in an “incident-related general address” (因事普說), and record masters being requested to give one after questioning or before the summer retreat. Yuejian Shanquan says, “I will give you all one general address” (為諸人普說一上), while another request specifies the subject with “give a general address on this” (普說此). The ordinary wording is thus institutionalized as a placarded public recorded-sayings genre with venue, occasion, audience, and questioning. Event, heading, and delivery are grammatical presentations of the same institution, not different lexical things.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 870 hits in 134 texts. Noun and verb constructions denote the same general-address event; the two former targets could not distinguish different referents without their explanations and are merged. The general-address placard (普說牌) names the placard for this genre, not another sense. General address remains distinct from ascending the hall (上堂), small gathering (小參), addressing the assembly (示眾), question-and-answer, and taking up the whisk.

Senses.Explanation: A communal summons calls the whole assembly to a shared assigned activity. Monastic regulations use it for collective labor and explain that all ranks share the work. Chan hall addresses reuse the same summons formula in “strike the drum and summon everyone to look”: look names the assigned action, while the headword still denotes the communal call. The institutional call remains the common referent across labor, attendance, and rhetorical reuse.

Senses.Explanation: 普賢 is Samantabhadra, a named figure repeatedly paired with Manjusri in the retained Chan passages. Huangbo Xiyun calls Manjusri real wisdom and Samantabhadra expedient wisdom, then says that ultimately there is neither real nor expedient wisdom, only one mind. Yongming Yanshou speaks of entering Samantabhadra's body of the dharma realm. Nanyang Huizhong calls Samantabhadra and Manjusri great persons and describes the matter before him as their sphere. These are descriptions assigned to the same named figure, not separate meanings of the name.

Senses.Explanation: The closing line of a stable verse, repeatedly quoted as a refusal to engage imposed discrimination or contrived explanation. Yongjue Yuanxian uses the expression through Yongjue directly answers a question about cutting off habitual dust with the paired verse lines ending in the headword. Muyun Tongmen independently deploys it through Muyun independently raises the same closing after asking why Snow Peak says he had already met the monks. Zuliang voices the line as his reply to an imagined challenge in an early morning instruction. Minshu applies the line to his own position after reviewing modes of Chan teaching.
